Oral evidence - 16 Nov 2026

Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy

Oral evidence: Space resilience, HC 572

Monday 16 November 2026

5.15 pm

Watch the meeting

Members present: Matt Western (The Chair); Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom; Catherine Atkinson; Lord Godson; Baroness Kidron; Helen Maguire; Lord Sedwill; Lord Tunnicliffe; Baroness Tyler of Enfield; Lord Watts.

Questions 23 - 29

Witnesses

Dr Michelle Howard, Defence and Space Policy Advisor, The D Group, Head of Defence, Space4Earth Capital; Nathan Mathiot, Director, Policy and Public Affairs, ADS Group; Major General Paul Tedman, former Commander of UK Space Command, Managing Director for European Space, Anduril Industries.

Examination of witnesses

Dr Michelle Howard, Nathan Mathiot and Major General Paul Tedman.

The Chair: Good afternoon, and a warm welcome to you. This is our second panel of our second session. I invite you to introduce yourselves.

Nathan Mathiot: I am director of policy and public affairs at ADS Group. We represent the UK’s civil aerospace, defence, security and space sectors. We have over 2,200 members and around 40% of those have what we would call a primary interest in the space sector—so a significant cohort of both small and large companies involved in the sector as a whole.

Dr Michelle Howard: I run the space working group at The D Group. I am the head of defence for space for Space4Earth Capital, which is a dual-use space tech growth fund. I was also the specialist adviser for the House of Lords UK Engagement with Space Committee.

Major General Paul Tedman: I am a simple soldier, recently retired. I spent about 25 years flying and fighting helicopters. Then in 2021 I went to US Space Command as our one-star in that enterprise, leading on US space policy, strategy and plans. I came back in 2022 on promotion and commanded UK Space Command until this summer, where I was responsible for all UK space policy, operations, training and capability development. Germane to this, I was one of the lead authors for the SDR space chapter. I led on the DIP capability development as part of the UK space strategy development.

The Chair: I was going to say that your reputation preceded you, but you did at least fill out some of your biography. Thank you for that.

Helen Maguire: There is obviously quite a huge reliance now on space-based infrastructure for defence—whether it is the digital targeting web or the missile warning system—and it is quite central to modern military effectiveness. This is a question for all of you but maybe we will start with you, Michelle. What is the most concerning dependence that you feel that our Armed Forces have on space-based infrastructure?

Dr Michelle Howard: There are a number to choose from, but I will begin with some of the capabilities that have suddenly come into question about our assured access. For example, with our military space-based assets, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance is obviously really important to track troop movements.

Military Satcom is particularly important—it is so important that the first act of war in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine was to disrupt and cyber attack Viasat’s satellite broadband internet access, thus disrupting Ukrainian command and control for the entire invasion. This for me is quite concerning, as it is for a lot of people in the defence space community, because assured access has suddenly been called into question.

There is not just that. In March 2025, the US suspended Ukrainian access to geospatial intelligence capabilities, thus disrupting their access to commercial satellite imagery platforms, Maxar Technologies. This stopped them being able to track Russian troop movements. In mid-October this year, without warning SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starshield, which is the military grade satellite comms infrastructure part of Starlink. This coincided with an increase in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure and Ukrainian cities. This essentially stops the Ukrainian military’s ability to interact and communicate with its drones, and so obviously it has left them quite defenceless. This is a real concern for me. I will stop there and let my colleagues pick that up, but I am happy to carry on.

Helen Maguire: That was great, thank you. As a former soldier, Major General Paul Tedman, could you answer that question as well?

Major General Paul Tedman: I would point to two things. I always like to talk of a triangle. If the tip of the triangle is space, you need to be able to control space to be able to get control of the air, which would sit under space in that triangle. If you cannot get control of the air, as Montgomery said in 1945, you lose the war and you lose it quickly. If you want a good example of that, it is Ukraine. There is no control of space, there is no control of the air, and it is a bloody mess in the land and the maritime environments.

The first point is that you have to be able to control the space domain. The second point is that, without space—we just assume space capabilities are available to the land, maritime and air environments—you would not be able to understand through space-based ISR; you would not be able to move through positioning, navigation and timing; you would not be able to communicate through satellite communications and data relays; and, ultimately, you would not be able to fight.

Helen Maguire: Brilliant, thank you. Nathan, do you have anything to add to that?

Nathan Mathiot: I think my colleagues have covered the bulk of it. All I would add is about assured access. I think we need to have assured access to launch, so we are able to replenish as part of the picture. There is the variety of different services that our military depend on, whether it is satcoms or missile awareness. It is the whole piece of trying to understand the battlefield, to communicate and to move in a co-ordinated fashion. Beyond that, it is the challenge of how we then replenish those services. I think it is a particular concern for the UK going forward.

Lord Sedwill: Picking up those points, we have already heard that the first action of the Russian invasion of Ukraine was a satellite attack to disrupt their military communications. We know that they use GPS jamming a great deal as well, which had a dramatic effect, for example, on the efficacy of GPS-guided shells. We know that the Russians themselves train to operate without access to satellites and space-based technology. As you have already set out, our own allies can restrict access to it. Major General Tedman, this question is probably for you first. How prepared are British forces to fight were we to lose access to our own or American space services? In your triangle, where does that differ?

Major General Paul Tedman: I think we will always be prepared to fight without space, going back to maps and compasses, but would we be efficient and effective? No. It is a simple answer, if you consider that 3,000 systems in an Army brigade rely on space-based systems. The former chief of space operations in the US put it really well. He said that if you did not assure space services for our armed forces, you would be talking about the multiple degrees of scale difference that we would need, and investment into those capabilities, because we just assume space is there and it makes us more efficient and effective. If we did not assure space for those capabilities and the land, maritime and air environment, the challenge would be that it would cost us a degree more and a scale more for our Armed Forces.

Lord Sedwill: If I can just pursue that, our Armed Forces are seeking to develop more autonomous, more hybrid capability. The First Sea Lord’s strategy of a hybrid Navy is probably the most advanced one, but the others are on the same kind of trajectory. Does that not increase our dependence on space and thus our vulnerability should those systems be disrupted by either an adversary or a kill switch from an ally?

Major General Paul Tedman: Yes is the short answer, and therefore there are two aspects to this, as I highlighted earlier: the things that we must assure for all of those systems to work in the other domains. This committee is about resilience but, if I may say so, we slightly overindex resilience. There are two aspects to deterrence: denial and punishment, as we heard earlier. Deterrence by denial involves having the capability and the will to use it. Do we have the capability and will to use some or all of our space systems and secure deterrence? Well, obviously not, because we are seeing all these acts in space and we are being challenged and contested.

Then you have deterrence by punishment. Are we capable of responding to the threats that we know are out there, and some of the actions, as you pointed out, Lord Sedwill? I would even go further and say that, three months prior to the invasion of Ukraine, Russia destroyed one of its own satellites in orbit, which you could take as a demonstration of capability. There are really obvious and clear threats, and Russia has proven an irrational actor. Do we have, first, the control and the capabilities to deter, and, secondly, should that deterrence fail—arguably we are close—are we resilient enough to be able to take a first-move punch, absorb it and still deliver those capabilities that are essential for our Armed Forces on the backside? That is a question that everyone should wrestle with.

Lord Sedwill: From the way in which you are posing that as a rather open question, it sounds as though you are not confidently telling us that the answer is yes.

Major General Paul Tedman: It is not a clear yes, Lord Sedwill.

Lord Sedwill: You mentioned the defence investment plan in your opening remarks on the space strategy. Assuming all of that is implemented, and at pace, et cetera, how close do we get to a yes? How close do we get to closing the gap that you have identified?

Major General Paul Tedman: I would say that the SDR provides good ends—the strategy—and the DIP closes with the means. It is the ways that I worry about. Are we going to get there sufficiently quickly to match the threat? Policy is free; the threat is not. Are we going to be able to match the threat, which is increasing exponentially? That is the bit that I am worried about: time.

Lord Sedwill: Dr Howard, please pick up any points that you would like to, but could I also ask you to focus on this allied point—the degree to which we can work with allies and to which we need to think about an alternative, if necessary, to our dependence on Starshield, et cetera?

Dr Michelle Howard: I will start by picking up the point about the integrated force 2030 because I am doing some work on it at the moment. It is worth highlighting that the point of the integrated force 2030 is to develop a future force structure that is more information-centric, that is automated and that consists of hybrid networks. Of course, this means that it is definitely more networked and it is autonomous, which requires space-based assets. So, yes, we are a lot more dependent. When we move into the future force structure, this focuses on deep precision strike, all underpinned by the digital targeting web.

What would space denial do in this future force structure? It would not stop our capability overnight, but it would progressively reduce our range for deep precision strike, tempo, precision, awareness, connectivity, and our operational integration across all five domains. That is the concern. Technically, we could still fight—regarding the ability to say yes, it is yes—but we would be far more vulnerable to adversaries who have maintained their space advantage. To come on to the—

Lord Sedwill: Sorry to interrupt, and do come on to your second point, but may I just clarify what you said there? It sounds as though what you are saying is that, sitting behind the entire SDR strategy of modernising the force, the digital targeting web, integrated capability and hybrid capability, is, in effect, a single point of failure, which is a dependence on space-based technology in order to enable all of that. Or am I overstating it?

Dr Michelle Howard: I do not want to say that you are overstating it but the ability to be as effective as we would like to be, as defined in that strategy, is heavily reliant on space in a way that is perhaps not appreciated.

Lord Sedwill: Thank you, and apologies for interrupting; do come to your second point.

Dr Michelle Howard: That is absolutely fine. I will quickly speak about the alliance point. Because of these issues of direct threats and assured access, even from our allied systems, there is now a huge discussion in policy circles and among industry about sovereignty, what that means and how we can start developing sovereign infrastructure. One thing that I would like to put to the committee is about developing a more slightly sophisticated debate about sovereign capability because of choices that we have made in the UK over decades and decades.

It is not in our gift to have entirely sovereign supply chains and sovereign capability, but what we are really asking is: how do we assure consistent and secure access to the capabilities that we acquire? If you are viewing it that way, there are a number of policy interventions that we can make, such as domestic design authority, so that, in order to update software in weapon systems, you do not have to go to a foreign country to request permission for that software update and can continue to use that platform; and localised IP manufacturing facilities so that we can reconstitute locally in the case of an attack.

These are really important points to focus on, as opposed to maintaining entirely sovereign capability, which would be quite difficult to get through. We will heavily rely on allied assistance for many years to come, in particular from the US; we are just so integrated into each other’s national security architecture. The US, in particular, is integrated into our defence and national security architecture. Simply deciding that we would like to pull US systems out of our architecture just would not work in the near term.

Lord Sedwill: On that shared sovereignty point, are there any non-sovereign capabilities on which we are dependent that are provided by—how can I put it?—non-allies other than NATO, Five Eyes, Japan. Are we dependent, for example, on Chinese technology—on technology from outside the close group of countries with which we work?

Dr Michelle Howard: It is not my area of expertise, but I know that, obviously, the microprocessor chips, semiconductors and rare earth minerals that go into our critical systems are certainly supplied by non-allies. But there is a whole level of supply chain provenance work that needs to be done in order to really understand the full extent of our vulnerabilities there.

Lord Sedwill: Thanks, Dr Howard. I turn to Mr Mathiot for the industry perspective. Please reflect on any of the questions or points that General Tedman or Dr Howard have raised. In particular, what do we need in terms of a government partnership with industry to address some of the vulnerabilities that we have just heard about?

Nathan Mathiot: There are a few components to this that my colleagues have already covered which I would agree with. First, the investments made in the defence investment plan, focused on space control and counterspace, are going in the right direction. What does industry need from government? There is a need for a more mature, strategic relationship between the two sides. The Government are increasingly becoming a key, anchor customer in the space market. With that come certain obligations in fostering the health of the sector. So, with a few things, there has been a bit of an overreliance and tendency towards offering grant funding towards the sector in the R&D space. There is a need to transition over time, not abruptly, towards more procurement of capability as a long-term customer to sustain a more robust industrial base as a whole.

There is an export dimension to this. I appreciate we are talking about the defence sphere, but defence space exports are a significant component and there needs to be a more properly resourced, robust export support regime. Part of this is to do with the internal changes within government. There have been machinery of government changes with the UK Space Agency and how it interacts with Space Command, which will inevitably always cause a tiny bit of friction in the system as government colleagues work through that.

The export support side is an integral part of providing a wider customer base beyond what the UK itself can ultimately offer. Then, the international partnerships piece that you were just probing is such a knotty subject. There is a sovereign capability discussion, on which I would agree with what Michelle said, that we need a more nuanced conversation there. There are things we clearly might want to have under sovereign control, there are things we might want to have assured access to and there are things we might want to buy from trusted partners. There are also things we might be quite happy to get from the commercial market, but we have to work with our partners.

I conclude that there are some opportunities for some particularly significant major space programmes, working with allies like Japan, for example, where we can make our limited budget—if we are being honest—go much further, notwithstanding the point that, of course, there are certain tensions in terms of dependencies that this can also introduce into the mix.

Lord Sedwill: Thank you. I was one of the authors of “allied by design” as a concept. Sovereign is fine, but we need to be able to work with trusted partners, as you said. Could I ask one final quick question of you? If you do not have the technical expertise, that is fine. To the best of your understanding, is there a practical, technical solution to some of these vulnerabilities? Is this a question of throwing enough resources at it to ensure assured access to GPS, communications, or whatever it might be, or is it simply the case that there is no technical solution that can avoid the spoofing, jamming and other disruptive techniques?

Nathan Mathiot: I think you are probably right to say I am not going to be the technical expert to offer an informed view on that. What I probably would say is that we feel you can achieve a degree of deterrence through resilience, and resilience comes through a number of different measures. I am not sure if this is something that boils to down to one singular capability area that we need to take in-house, or we need to harden and make resilient, or we need to provide a terrestrial alternative.

The UK is pursuing lots of different bets. On the PNT side, we are exploring terrestrial solutions. We are exploring how we work with Eutelsat OneWeb in offering a diversity of options in a space where there are predominant players, to have a mixture of options to drive forward the overall level of resilience. This will thereby raise the level of uncertainty for our adversaries that they can have a decisive impact if they wish to escalate into the space domain, for which, given all the conversation in the previous panel around debris, comes with certain consequences—for example, whether it is worth it for all parties involved that are not necessarily manifest in the other domains, militarily speaking.

Lord Sedwill: Thank you—fascinating.

The Chair: I am afraid we are going to have a hard stop at 5.50 pm, if colleagues could bear that in mind, for us to remain quorate.

Lord Godson: Thank you, Chair, and thanks to all of you for your testimonies. We have not actually yet had an overview today of the sources of threat for space conflict. I would like to hear from all of you on your views on that. We have rightly heard about Russia specifically, but I would also like to hear more about China and other sorts of threats, not least in the light of the number of self-destructions of bits of kit that we have had referred to in the previous session and today’s.

Secondly, I would like also your view of the success of government in educating both the public and indeed Whitehall and the other services—services in the wider sense—about these threats. Perhaps in that connection, in the light of the general’s own distinguished career, I would like to hear whether the star level and the status level of Space Command should be raised further—which might perhaps have helped your pension in some ways. But it is a genuine question, about what more can be done to raise the status of space within the national security cosmos.

Major General Paul Tedman: Thank you. I will go first and then open it up to my colleagues. On the space threats, people generally talk to a continuum from non-kinetic reversible jamming, just disruption of space capabilities, all the way through to exo-atmospheric nuclear explosions on orbit. In between, there are capabilities that can grapple other satellites. There are direct ascent anti-satellite missiles that launch from terrestrial sites into orbit. Most, if not all, of those capabilities have been demonstrated and are real. Russia has put a stated intent out that it wishes to put a nuclear weapon on orbit, which would break all sorts of international obligations. That range of capabilities is not science fiction any more; it all exists. If it is not on orbit, it could be on orbit. I think that is probably about as much as we can say in a sort of unclassified setting. In terms of education—

Lord Godson: Could I just ask about China as well?

Major General Paul Tedman: Sorry, I beg your pardon. The difference between Russia and China is, as I mentioned earlier, I still think Russia is an irrational actor. We have seen it do all sorts of things that we did not think a rational country or leadership would do. China is far more dependent on space than perhaps Russia is. Russia has not embraced the space domain to the degree that western powers have or indeed China has. China is far more sophisticated in its capabilities on orbit, but is more of a rational actor, if that makes sense.

To simplify it—as I said, simple soldier—China has greater capability but is more rational. Russia has less capability but is irrational. The two together pose us a problem. But they have increased their counterspace arsenal by 70% since 2021 as two nations, a significant increase in counterspace capabilities.

Lord Godson: And what of educating the public, educating the public and the status of the Space Command?

Major General Paul Tedman: We try our level best. Part of the challenge is that space people advocating for space only gets you so far. My observation from the US was that when the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff stood up and said that our most important domain is space, people started paying attention. When the commander of the Indo-Pacific said, “My most important domain to invest in is space because I cannot get out of port without being seen by Chinese ISR”, then people start to pay attention.

From a military perspective, it leads to your third question of whether we should grow Space Command. Of course the answer to that is yes, but my point would be that defence needs to undertake a journey, where it understands and considers space as part of multidomain operations. You could say that land, maritime and air are very well understood but space and cyber are not understood. When we said we were going to do multidomain operations, did we increase the size of the defence budget, for example, to accommodate two brand new domains? The answer was no. We have kept the same broad defence budget but increased to five domains. There is a challenge within defence and wider government in integrating space into our thinking.

Others can comment on the public. We have done “days without space” for Ministers and elements of the public on what that would mean. There were some great questions earlier about what it would look like for UK if we disrupted capabilities to the nation for a day. As we heard, 20% of the economy is reliant on space. Figures say that it would cost our economy £1 billion a day if we just disrupted the timing signal. It would be significant; there is no doubt about it.

Dr Michelle Howard: I am happy to pick up on public education, starting with a relatively sobering statistic: a UK Space public attitudes survey came out relatively recently and found that the first word that 21% of the UK public associated with space was “aliens” and only 8% thought about communications and connectivity. This highlights how far we have to go. We do a lot of work trying to develop a conversation with the public, but it is quite difficult to demonstrate the integral nature of our UK space capabilities without being inherently boring. The things that really inspire people are the astronauts and the rocket launches—that is what people want to show up to. Trying to be advocates for space as Trojan horses in different conferences that are about investment, transport or logistics is probably the best way that we can advocate to the public and the policy-making community about the importance of space. You are seeing it in the investment community, where there is a lot of private capital interest in space. But in the wider population we still have a long way to go.

The Chair: I am afraid I will have to move us on now.

Lord Watts: What more can the Government do to support companies in the defence sector to be more resilient and to improve the security of the products, and which space-based systems and services should the Government be looking to prioritise for public expenditure?

Nathan Mathiot: Fundamentally there is a wider conversation about the defence investment plan and the national debate on reaching 3% of GDP on defence expenditure and then 3.5%. From an industrial perspective, the reason we keep banging on about this is because of the confidence that that would give to companies to invest here in the UK, and that applies equally to the defence space sector as a subcategory of that. The customer is given the outline figures, but we need that year-by-year breakdown of the pipeline to encourage investment in resilient capabilities.

Lord Watts: I asked what you would pick out for public investment.

Nathan Mathiot: I would pick out launch capability as a particular area where we can see that there is a bottleneck in existing dependence, for example, on SpaceX capacity. The UK and Europe as a whole need to strengthen their own launch capabilities.

Dr Michelle Howard: I am conscious of time, so my answer will be simple. Clear strategic intent and a contract pipeline would be the best thing Government could do to support our defence space industrial base.

Lord Watts: Which priorities?

Dr Michelle Howard: I dare not say which, although ISAM—in-orbit servicing and manufacturing—is a real area of strategic strength for us. It is worth Government leaning into that and developing and focusing on those capabilities.

Major General Paul Tedman: Again, I will keep it short. It goes back to a question asked in the previous session, and I think that very clear leadership from Government about who is in charge would be super helpful. I think there were three Secretaries of State associated with the UK space strategy, but who is actually in charge? The governance was covered. There is a lot of work to do in procurement and acquisition reform. The NAD has a clear mandate, and, after that, we just need to accelerate it.

In terms of capability priorities, it is very clear in all the documentation sets that the capability we are underinvesting in is space control. It links to Michelle’s point; it is adjacent to ISAM, so the two are linked. That is clear in the DIT and in the SDR, and it is also clear in the space strategy. So there is a very clear signal to industry, which I am now part of, where we need to invest.

Lord Watts: This is a yes or no question: do you think we should procure only from our allies?

Major General Paul Tedman: No, it is both. I think we need to diversify but not divorce from our closest allies in space.

Dr Michelle Howard: Yes, we should procure national security assets only from our allies.

Nathan Mathiot: Yes, the same as Michelle.

The Chair: Thank you so much for the session this afternoon. That concludes our second panel of our second session. I really appreciate the quality and the information that you have shared with us this afternoon. Thank you.
